House Robber II (houses in a circle)
The first and last houses are adjacent, so they cannot both be robbed: solve the linear problem twice, once without the last house and once without the first. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Decode Ways ("226" → 3)
Like Climbing Stairs, but each step (one or two digits) is only allowed when it forms a valid letter. Zeros are the trap: "0" alone is invalid and "06" is not 6. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Partition Equal Subset Sum

A 0/1 knapsack on booleans: can some subset reach sum/2? Iterating s downwards stops a number from being reused within the same round. O(n · sum) time, O(sum) space. "Target Sum" (+/− signs) reduces to the same subset-sum count.
Coin Change II: number of ways to make the amount

Looping coins in the outer loop counts each combination once ({1,2} and {2,1} are the same). Swapping the loops counts permutations instead (Combination Sum IV). Forward iteration allows unlimited use of each coin, the opposite of 0/1 knapsack. O(n · amount).
Minimum Path Sum in a Grid

dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(top, left), compressed to one row because each cell only needs the row above and the cell to its left. O(R·C) time, O(C) space. This space-optimisation step is a common follow-up for any 2D grid DP.
Longest Palindromic Subsequence

Interval DP: matching ends add 2 to the inside answer, otherwise drop one end. Fill i from the right so the shorter intervals are ready. O(n²) time and space. Equivalent to LCS(s, reverse(s)). "Minimum insertions to make a palindrome" = n − LPS.
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown (state machine DP)

Model each day as a set of states with transitions. The same template solves all stock variants: unlimited trades (drop the cooldown), with a fee (subtract it on sell), or at most k trades (one hold/sold pair per transaction). O(n) time, O(1) space.
Maximal Square (largest square of 1s)
A square ending at a cell is limited by the smallest square ending at its top, left and top-left neighbours. O(R·C) time. Returning area, not side length, is a frequent slip.
Memoization (top-down) vs tabulation (bottom-up)

| Memoization | Tabulation
Written as | Recursion + cache (array or HashMap) | Loops filling a table
States computed | Only those reachable from the start | All states, in a fixed order
Order of evaluation | Handled by recursion | You must find it (smaller first)
Stack depth | O(depth); deep inputs can overflow | None
Space optimisation | Hard | Easy: keep only the rows you read
Speed in Java | Call overhead, boxing if HashMap | Usually faster
Rule of thumb: write the recurrence first, memoise it to get a correct answer fast, then convert to tabulation if asked for less space or no recursion.
0/1 knapsack vs unbounded knapsack: why the loop direction flips

| 0/1 (each item once) | Unbounded (reuse items)
1D inner loop | Capacity from high to low | Capacity from low to high
Why | dp[c - w] must still be the old row (item not used yet) | dp[c - w] may already include this item, which is allowed
Examples | Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum | Coin Change, Coin Change II
Time / space | O(n · W) / O(W) | O(n · W) / O(W)
Interview tip: if you go upward in a 0/1 problem, an item gets used twice and the answer is silently wrong. Explain the direction; interviewers ask.
Counting combinations vs permutations: which loop goes outside?

| Coins outer, amount inner | Amount outer, coins inner
Counts | Combinations: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same | Permutations: 1+2 and 2+1 are different
Problem | Coin Change II | Combination Sum IV, Climbing Stairs with steps {1, 2}
For amount 3, coins {1, 2} | 2 ({1,1,1}, {1,2}) | 3 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1)
Rule of thumb: putting coins outside fixes the order in which coins are considered, so each multiset is counted once. Swap the loops only when order should count.
Full 2D table vs rolling rows vs a single 1D array

| Full m × n table | Two rows (prev, cur) | One 1D array
Space | O(m · n) | O(n) | O(n)
Can rebuild the solution (not just its value) | Yes, backtrack through the table | No | No
Works when a cell reads | Anything | Previous row only | Previous row and the left cell; needs a saved "diagonal" for LCS / Edit Distance
Examples | Print the actual LCS string | Edit Distance | Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum
Interview tip: solve with the full table first. Then say which cells each cell depends on; that tells you how many rows you can drop.
